hook: *$110B* merger just created a new media giant
dek: Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery are now one company called Skydance.

slides.label: What happened
slides.text: Paramount officially closed its *$110 billion* acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The combined company is now called *Skydance*.

slides.label: Who's under one roof
slides.text: HBO, CBS News, CNN, and major film studios from both companies now sit under *Skydance*.

slides.label: How we got here
slides.text: Paramount beat out *Netflix* in a months-long bidding war for WBD before locking in the deal back in February.

slides.label: The pushback
slides.text: Lawmakers and Hollywood talent criticized the deal, warning about the *impact of media consolidation*.

slides.label: Last hurdle cleared
slides.text: Last month, Paramount settled with *12 states* that sued to block the merger over antitrust concerns.

slides.label: The fine print
slides.text: Skydance must release *30 theatrical films* in its first two years and spend *$300 million more* on US production than both companies spent last year combined.

slides.label: Who's running it
slides.text: *David Ellison* leads Skydance alongside *Ynon Kreiz*, the former chairman and CEO of Mattel.

slides.label: Why it matters
slides.text: Fewer companies now control more of what gets greenlit and aired, which raises the stakes for creators outside the usual gatekept circles.

question: Good for the industry or bad for competition? One word.

caption_instagram:
Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery just completed a $110 billion merger, forming a new company called Skydance that now controls HBO, CBS News, CNN and major film studios.

The deal almost didn't happen. Paramount had to out-compete Netflix for WBD, survive criticism from lawmakers and Hollywood talent over consolidation, and settle with 12 states that sued to block it over antitrust concerns. Part of that settlement forces Skydance to release at least 30 theatrical films in its first two years and spend $300 million more on US production than both companies spent last year combined. David Ellison now leads Skydance alongside Ynon Kreiz, former chairman and CEO of Mattel.

Fewer, bigger gatekeepers controlling more of what gets made and aired is worth watching, especially for creators still trying to get a foot in the door.

Good for the industry or bad for competition? One word.

caption_linkedin:
Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery have officially completed their $110 billion merger, creating Skydance, a company now controlling HBO, CBS News, CNN, and major film studios.

What stands out operationally is the settlement that cleared the deal. To resolve antitrust lawsuits from 12 states, Skydance agreed to release at least 30 theatrical films over the next two years and spend $300 million more on US production than Paramount and WBD spent combined last year. That's a rare case where regulatory pushback directly shaped a company's production commitments, not just its deal terms.

David Ellison now leads Skydance alongside Ynon Kreiz, the former chairman and CEO of Mattel, betting that scale and reach can outcompete streaming rivals.

For founders and operators, this is a reminder that consolidation reshapes who controls distribution and access, which matters most for those building outside the biggest platforms.

Good for the industry or bad for competition? One word.
